title: Dendritic Spinule Dynamics, Regulation, and Function
abstract: Dendritic spines are neuronal structures known to be involved in synaptic plasticity, connectivity, and communication. Disruptions in spine shape, size, and number may contribute to the development of neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease and schizophrenia. Spinules are thin dendritic spine protrusions, and can be small, transient, and motile, or elongated and stabilized by contacting other neuronal elements. These protrusions are often induced and enhanced by neuronal activity and are commonly found in healthy brain tissue. However, how spinule morphology and dynamics relate to their function and role in neuropsychiatric disease are unknown. Neurons from a mouse model were chemically transfected with various fluorescent proteins and plasmids. FM dyes were used to label presynaptic terminals of axons, a possible contact for dendritic spinules. These techniques were performed for future fluorescent imaging and visualization of the neuron cultures. High-speed 3D structured illumination microscopy (SIM) and enhanced resolution confocal microscopy were used to image the neuronal cultures and observe spinule dynamics and morphology over time. The data reveals that there are two classes of spinules: short-lived and long-lived. Induced neuronal activation increased spinule number per spine and contacts with distal neuronal elements. Specifically, activity-induced, long-lived spinules extend towards and contact presynaptic terminals, and this may play a role in secondary synapse formation. The data suggest that spinules may facilitate neuronal connectivity, and that spinule dysfunction may be associated with neuropsychiatric disorders.
